summary: Sirach 6 begins with warnings about speech, self-exaltation, and the damage a wicked soul brings on itself. It then teaches how to test friendship, praises the rare value of a faithful friend, and turns to a long appeal to seek wisdom through discipline, listening, and attachment to wise teachers.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins two major concerns of Sirach: trustworthy relationships and lifelong formation in wisdom. It shows that wisdom is not presented as quick information but as disciplined learning that reshapes speech, friendship, and desire.

context.author: Yeshua, or Jesus, son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; the Greek translation was made later by his unnamed grandson.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews in Egypt or the wider diaspora through the grandson's translation.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal learning, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture in the background.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction: poetic teaching, maxims, comparisons, and direct address from a teacher to a learner.

outline.heading: Speech and Self-Damage
outline.note: The chapter warns against becoming an enemy instead of a friend, against a double tongue, and against self-exaltation that leaves a person ruined.

outline.heading: Testing Friendship
outline.note: Pleasant speech may multiply friends, but the teacher urges caution because some friends vanish or turn hostile when hardship comes.

outline.heading: The Faithful Friend
outline.note: A faithful friend is described as defense, treasure, medicine, and a gift found by those who fear the Lord.

outline.heading: Wisdom Requires Patient Labor
outline.note: The student is told to gather instruction from youth onward; wisdom is pictured as cultivation that bears fruit, but also as harsh and difficult for the unlearned.

outline.heading: Accepting Wisdom's Bonds
outline.note: The teacher urges the learner to accept wisdom's fetters and chain, promising that what feels burdensome will become rest, gladness, strength, and honor.

outline.heading: Seeking Wise Instruction
outline.note: The chapter closes by calling the willing learner to listen, attach himself to the wise, seek understanding early, and meditate on the Lord's ordinances and commandments.

keyVerses.text: A faithful friend is a strong defense. He who has found him has found a treasure.
keyVerses.why: This sentence anchors the chapter's central contrast between unreliable companions and the rare value of a faithful friend.

keyVerses.text: My son, gather instruction from your youth up. Even when you have gray hair you will find wisdom.
keyVerses.why: This begins the chapter's turn from friendship to lifelong education in wisdom.

keyVerses.text: Search and seek, and she will be made known to you. When you get hold of her, don’t let her go.
keyVerses.why: It summarizes the active pursuit of wisdom: the learner must search, seek, grasp, and remain with her.

keyVerses.text: Let your mind dwell on the ordinances of the Lord and meditate continually on his commandments. He will establish your heart and your desire for wisdom will be given to you.
keyVerses.why: The final verse connects the pursuit of wisdom with sustained attention to the Lord's ordinances and commandments.

themes: the value of a faithful friend

questions.question: Why does the chapter start with a warning about becoming an enemy instead of a friend?
questions.answer: The opening treats damaged relationship as a serious outcome of speech and character. Verse 1 links an evil name, shame, reproach, sin, and a double tongue, so the concern is not only having enemies but becoming the kind of person whose speech destroys trust.

questions.question: What is a “double tongue”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in verse 1 beside becoming an enemy instead of a friend. In this chapter's own terms, it points to speech that creates shame and reproach rather than trustworthy friendship. The verse does not give a technical definition, so it is safest to read it as unreliable or divided speech within relationships.

questions.question: What does the image of a dry tree mean?
questions.answer: Verses 2-4 use images of self-ruin: a soul torn like a bull, leaves eaten up, fruit destroyed, and a person left like a dry tree. The point is that self-exaltation and wickedness do not merely harm others; they also consume the person who practices them.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying to distrust everyone?
questions.answer: No. Verse 6 says to let many be at peace with you, but to have very few advisers. The chapter distinguishes broad peaceful relations from deep trust, which should be tested over time and especially in hardship.

questions.question: Why does hardship matter so much for friendship here?
questions.answer: Verses 7-12 repeatedly contrast ordinary companionship with the “day of your affliction.” Some friends are present for an occasion or at the table but do not remain when the person is brought low. The chapter treats adversity as a test that reveals whether friendship is durable or only convenient.

questions.question: What does “Those who fear the Lord will find him” mean in the friendship section?
questions.answer: Verse 16 says a faithful friend is “a life-saving medicine,” and then says those who fear the Lord will find him. Verse 17 adds that the one who fears the Lord directs friendship properly. The chapter connects reverence for the Lord with wise conduct in friendship, without claiming that every faithful person will always find many trustworthy friends quickly.

questions.question: Why is wisdom pictured with fetters, chains, and bonds?
questions.answer: Verses 24-25 use restraint imagery: feet in fetters, neck in a chain, shoulder under a burden, and bonds that must be borne. But verses 28-31 reverse the image: the same fetters and chains become rest, gladness, strength, glory, ornament, and a crown. The chapter presents wisdom's discipline as hard at first but ultimately life-giving and honorable.

questions.question: Who is the “her” in the wisdom section?
questions.answer: From verse 19 onward, wisdom is referred to as “her” and “she.” This matches the chapter's personified presentation of wisdom as someone to approach, seek, hold, and not let go. Readers differ on how far to press the personification: some read it mainly as poetic teaching, while later Jewish and Christian readers may connect it to broader traditions about Wisdom.

questions.question: How does the chapter say a learner becomes wise?
questions.answer: The closing verses emphasize willingness, listening, and seeking out wise company. The learner is told to love hearing, incline the ear, stand among elders, attach himself to the wise, listen to godly discourse, and meditate on the Lord's ordinances and commandments.

glossary.def: A phrase in verse 1 for speech that belongs with shame, reproach, and damaged friendship; the chapter does not define it more technically.
The situation in verse 7 where a potential friend is proved before deep trust is given.
The trusted companion praised in verses 14-16 as defense, treasure, and life-saving medicine.
The restraints named in verse 24 as an image for wisdom's discipline; later the same restraints become symbols of strength and honor.
The Lord's ordered commands or requirements in verse 37, paired there with commandments as the focus of continual meditation.
